subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Processes of memory: encoding, storage and retrieval
The multi-store model and types of memory
Memory as an active process (Bartlett's War of the Ghosts)
Factors affecting the accuracy of memory

questions.q: In memory, what does 'encoding' refer to?
options: Converting information into a form that can be held in memory
Keeping information in memory over a period of time
Recovering information from storage when it is needed
Losing information that is no longer useful
questions.explain: Encoding is the process of changing sensory input into a form (visual, acoustic or semantic) that memory can store.

questions.q: Which of the following lists three ways information can be encoded?
questions.explain: Information can be encoded visually (as images), acoustically (as sounds) or semantically (by meaning).

questions.q: A student is asked to name the capital of France and answers 'Paris'. Which memory process is mainly being used at this moment?
questions.explain: Retrieval is the process of recovering stored information from memory when it is needed.

questions.q: Maria tries to remember a page by picturing where the diagrams and headings sit on it. Which type of encoding is she mainly using?
questions.explain: Remembering the appearance or layout of something relies on visual encoding.

questions.q: Who proposed the multi-store model of memory?
questions.explain: The multi-store model was put forward by Atkinson and Shiffrin in 1968.

questions.q: According to the multi-store model, in what order does information flow through the stores?
options: Sensory register, then short-term memory, then long-term memory
Short-term memory, then sensory register, then long-term memory
Long-term memory, then short-term memory, then sensory register
Sensory register, then long-term memory, then short-term memory
questions.explain: Information passes from the sensory register to short-term memory and then to long-term memory.

questions.q: What is the approximate capacity of short-term memory?
questions.explain: Miller found the capacity of short-term memory to be around 7 plus or minus 2 items, the 'magic number'.

questions.q: What is the approximate duration of short-term memory without rehearsal?
options: Less than a fifth of a second
questions.explain: Without rehearsal, information in short-term memory lasts roughly 18 to 30 seconds.

questions.q: In the multi-store model, which process transfers information from the sensory register into short-term memory?
questions.explain: Paying attention to information allows it to pass from the sensory register into short-term memory.

questions.q: According to the multi-store model, how is information transferred from short-term memory to long-term memory?
questions.explain: Maintenance rehearsal moves information from short-term memory into long-term memory.

questions.q: Which type of long-term memory stores personal experiences and events from your own life?
questions.explain: Episodic memory holds personal events and experiences, often linked to a particular time and place.

questions.q: Ben can ride a bicycle smoothly without consciously thinking about how to balance or pedal. Which type of memory is he relying on?
questions.explain: Procedural memory stores skills and actions that are carried out automatically, such as riding a bike.

questions.q: Knowing that Paris is the capital of France and that a triangle has three sides are examples of which type of memory?
questions.explain: Semantic memory stores general knowledge and facts about the world.

questions.q: Which study did Bartlett use to investigate reconstructive memory?
questions.explain: Bartlett (1932) used the 'War of the Ghosts' folk tale to demonstrate that memory is reconstructive.

questions.q: What is a schema?
options: A mental framework of knowledge and expectations that influences how we remember
A store that holds information for a lifetime
The process of converting information ready for storage
A precise, unchanging copy of an event
questions.explain: A schema is a package of prior knowledge and expectations that shapes, and can distort, what we recall.

questions.q: Bartlett's term 'effort after meaning' describes how people tend to:
options: Change unfamiliar information so it fits with what already makes sense to them
Rehearse information to move it into long-term memory
Store information in an exact, photographic form
Pay attention to information in the sensory register
questions.explain: 'Effort after meaning' is the tendency to alter recall so unfamiliar material fits our existing understanding.

questions.q: When recalling 'The War of the Ghosts', British participants often changed the word 'canoes' to 'boats'. This best illustrates that memory is:
options: Reconstructive and influenced by existing schemas
An exact recording of the original event
Stored only acoustically in short-term memory
questions.explain: Changing unfamiliar details to familiar ones shows memory is reconstructed to fit the person's own schemas.

questions.q: Which of the following is a factor that can affect the accuracy of memory?
questions.explain: Interference, context and false memories are all factors that can affect the accuracy of memory.

questions.q: What is meant by 'interference' as a factor affecting memory?
options: When one memory disrupts the ability to recall another, often similar, memory
When the setting at recall matches the setting at learning
When we recall an event that never actually happened
When information moves from short-term to long-term memory
questions.explain: Interference occurs when memories, especially similar ones, disrupt one another and reduce recall accuracy.

questions.q: A diver learns a list of words underwater and later recalls more of them when tested underwater than on land. This best illustrates:
options: Context affecting the accuracy of memory
The limited capacity of short-term memory
questions.explain: Recall improves when the context at retrieval matches the context at learning, showing context-dependent memory.
